title: Murder in Stoney Creek: SIU release shocking details from the night a landlord shot and killed his tenants
subtitle: Double-homicide sparked lengthy standoff that led to fatal police shooting
article: A tenant and his landlord were arguing in the side yard of a home in east Stoney Creek on an evening in late May.
The landlord goes inside the house for a moment and returns with a gun. The tenant puts his hands up and looks toward the residence - home to both he and his fiancée as well as the landlord.
The landlord shoots him twice and the man falls to the ground.
The tenant's fiancée, who is standing nearby, runs over to her partner. More shots are fired.
She runs onto the road, followed by the landlord who continues to shoot at her. She collapses. The landlord, standing over her, shoots her again before walking back into the home.
Hamilton police are flooded with 911 calls. Hours later, after a standoff, the landlord is fatally shot by the lone round discharged by a police officer that day.

These are just some details contained in a report released by the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) on Monday that sheds light on what happened the night of the double homicide and subsequent police shooting that saw residents ordered to stay inside as emergency responders descended on their quiet neighbourhood.
The SIU investigates incidents involving police in Ontario in which someone dies. In his report, SIU director Joseph Martino said the officer was justified in using lethal force against the landlord.

According to the report, the landlord - who The Spectator previously identified as Terry Brekka - shot and killed his two tenants outside of 322 Jones Rd., a property he owned just north of Barton Street shortly before 5:40 p.m. on May 27.

Neither police nor the SIU have ever named the landlord. The tenants were later identified by Hamilton police as Carissa MacDonald, 27, and Aaron Stone, 28. The couple had planned to move out of the home in the coming days.
The report says the trio had a "falling out" over "who was going to pay for damage done to some property."
What transpired outside the home was caught on video and detailed to police by 911 callers.
Among those callers was a witness who reported seeing Brekka briefly chase a blood-soaked MacDonald before shooting her on the street.

The first officers on scene set up a perimeter around the home, as well as a command post in a nearby parking lot. Crisis negotiators and the Hamilton police emergency response unit (ERU), including the force's armoured tactical vehicle, were called.
"There ensued an hours-long standoff in the course of which negotiators attempted, with limited success, to reach the (landlord) inside the home," states the report.
In conversation with police, Brekka asked if his tenants were dead and for his apology to be passed on to their families. He also spoke to members of his own family throughout the night.
"He repeatedly apologized for what he had done, indicated he would not emerge from his predicament alive and suggested he would fight the police," the report notes.
In the course of the operation, officers learned Brekka was a registered owner of multiple handguns and rifles, as well as potentially unregistered firearms.

A pair of Scorpion carbine pistols, a DPMS Panther Arms rifle and modified detachable magazines used with the pistols were among the guns and ammunition later found inside the home, according to the report.
Both types of firearms are prohibited in Canada. The guns are believed to have been used in the shooting, the report states.
The police officer at the centre of the SIU investigation was a member of the ERU who was inside the armoured vehicle.

Roughly four hours after the tenants were shot, Brekka fired multiple rounds at the vehicle from inside his home. Twenty minutes later, he released another volley of shots through the front door, says the report.
That was when the police officer, who was behind the turret hatch of the armoured vehicle, fired a single round from his rifle at the front door.

The gunfire from the home stopped immediately. Police sent a robot inside, which captured video of the scene - including of Brekka face-down on the floor of the garage between a coffee table and a couch. There was blood around him.
Police attempted to talk to Brekka through the robot, but the 57-year-old didn't respond. He also didn't move when the robot grabbed his left foot.
Brekka was pronounced dead at the scene just before midnight. An autopsy cites a "gunshot wound to the torso" as the cause.

Martino, the SIU director, noted negotiations prior to the police shooting had "not proven fruitful" and there was "no reason to believe that continued negotiations might turn a corner or that retreat was possible" without potentially endangering the lives of those in the area.

"The officer had every reason to believe that his life, and the life of third parties, was in imminent peril and that responsive force was required to defend against loss of life or grievous bodily harm," Martino wrote.
"There is no doubt that the (officer) acted to defend himself, his colleagues and the general public from a reasonably apprehended attack when he shot the (landlord)," he added.
